questions.question: Using capital and fixed assets as examples, show that the informal and formal sectors run on the same accounting concepts in different forms.
questions.expected_answer: Capital is the owner's resources committed to the business: the supermarket owner deposits R600 000 into a business bank account recorded in a Capital account, while the spaza owner starts with R4 000 saved in cash — same concept, banked-and-recorded versus cash-and-remembered. Fixed assets are possessions kept for use, not sale: the supermarket's shelving, tills and vehicle mirror the spaza's fridge and table. The concepts are identical; only the recording differs.

questions.question: Explain the R350 leak in Ma Dlamini's month and what it teaches about why formal businesses record every expense.
questions.expected_answer: Her head held the big numbers — R5 200 in, R3 400 of stock — and estimated R1 800 profit. The notebook added the small expenses: taxi R175, electricity R110, airtime R65, giving true profit of R1 450. The R350 was always being spent; memory just could not hold it, so it leaked and inflated apparent profit. Formal recording exists because no memory holds a hundred small expenses, and decisions made on wrong numbers become wrong decisions.

questions.question: Match the stokvel to at least three modern accounting procedures and state the conclusion this comparison supports.
questions.expected_answer: Regular member contributions are capital formation; the member list and payout roster are a ledger of contributions and claims; the treasurer's report to members is financial reporting and accountability; rules about missed payments are credit control. The conclusion: modern accounting principles echo practices communities have used for generations — the subject formalises familiar instincts rather than importing foreign ones.
